So why am I telling you all this?

Because I spent years thinking something was wrong with me. That if I could just communicate better, be less sensitive, shrink myself a little more, maybe I’d finally fit their mold.

But the truth is, some environments aren’t broken by accident. They’re maintained on purpose. And the person who refuses to pretend everything is fine will always be framed as the disruption.

I’m not sharing this for sympathy. I’m sharing it because I know some of you are sitting in the middle of a family situation right now wondering why doing the right thing keeps costing you so much.

You’re not crazy. You’re just awake in a room full of people who agreed a long time ago to employ avoidance as the natural way to process wrongdoing. 

What shifted things for me wasn’t getting the apology I deserved or the moment where everyone finally understood me. It was deciding that my healing wasn’t contingent on their acknowledgment.

The generational stuff stops here. Not because I’m special, but because I’m willing. Shannon and I are trying to build something different. A home where hard conversations are welcome. Where no one has to earn the right to be heard. Where feelings aren’t ranked by who’s in favour that week.

That’s the vision. That’s what I’m working toward.

If you’re the black sheep in your family too, this one’s for you. You’re not the problem. You might just be the beginning of something healthier.

caption:
From the beginning, we made one decision clear: don’t let the physical lead the relationship. When you remove the pressure to hit physical milestones in your relationship, you create space to actually know each other. Emotionally. Spiritually. Intentionally. It was also so refreshing when we both felt the need to set this boundary in our spirits and confirmed it in conversation before we dated. Out the gate, we felt aligned because there wasn’t guilt or a power imbalance because we were already on the same page about something!

That doesn’t mean this is for everyone or that we judge others for their choices around physical intimacy, but waiting until marriage forced us to build a foundation that could stand on its own. We learned how to communicate instead of compensate. How to pursue connection instead of chemistry. How to practice self-control together rather than rely on just our feelings to carry the relationship forward.

In a world that replaces phones, values, and relationships every few years, choosing restraint is countercultural. But restraint isn’t repression, it’s direction. Make no mistake, it was very DIFFICULT, but difficulty isn’t a sign something is wrong; often it’s proof something matters. Also thank you Jesus for strength on the hard days!

What obedience protects, commitment gets to fully enjoy. And how sweet it was to have something to experience for the first time on our big day!

#firstkiss #intimacy #marriage #couples #christianlife

caption:
3 things to do to cherish your engagement season 💍

Prioritize date nights throughout your wedding planning:

Wedding planning will consume you if you let it. Protect your time together that has nothing to do with venues, vendors, or vows. Date nights keep you connected to the person, not just the event.

Document everything, photos, videos, every milestone big and small:

You will forget more than you think. The first venue you toured. The moment you said yes to the dress. The random Tuesday you stayed up laughing about nothing. Capture it. Future you will be grateful.

Experience something you’ve never experienced together:

Your engagement season is a once-in-a-lifetime window. Do something new, a day trip, an experience, something that becomes unique to this season that you’ll remember always. Start your marriage with a memory only the two of you share.

The wedding is one day. The engagement season is a chapter. 

Make it count. 

Engaged couples, what’s one thing you’re doing to make your engagement season memorable?

For some couples that means separation, being disowned, not inviting parents to the wedding, or stepping away from environments that refuse to respect the covenant. 

Marriage isn’t about keeping everyone comfortable, it’s about building a new family under God with loyalty, protection, and leadership. When others are committed to finding fault in the person God chose to walk life with you, when they’ve done nothing wrong to others, drawing a line isn’t rebellion, it’s biblical alignment.

caption:
I wasn’t ready to date until I recognized these 4 truths about love + relationships 👇

1️⃣ Don’t doctor an outcome. Real relationships aren’t built on forcing a connection or trying to make someone fit into your idea of love. When it’s right, it feels natural, like it’s unfolding effortlessly instead of being pushed. Love that’s authentic doesn’t need manipulation, it just is.

2️⃣ Love yourself first. If you don’t genuinely accept and care for who you are, you’ll always look for someone else to fill that gap. The healthiest relationships start with self-love, because the way you treat yourself sets the tone for how others treat you. You can’t build lasting love on a shaky foundation of insecurity.

3️⃣ Your partner should compliment you, not complete you. A relationship isn’t about finding your “other half”you’re already whole. The right partner amplifies your strengths and walks beside you, but they can’t erase emptiness or fix what you refuse to face. Real love is two complete people building something greater together.

4️⃣ Own your past. If your last relationship failed, it wasn’t only about what they did, it’s also about how you showed up. Taking responsibility for your part gives you clarity, closure, and the chance to grow. Without ownership, you risk repeating the same patterns in your next love story.

Whether you’re dating, married, or still healing, these truths can shift your perspective and create stronger, healthier relationships.

caption:
In a transactional relationship, love becomes a ledger. Every action is measured, every effort weighed against what’s received in return. It’s a mindset that says, “I’ll show up for you if you show up for me,” which slowly erodes trust and intimacy. Over time, this tit-for-tat dynamic can turn love into obligation, where connection is maintained only when terms feel fair. While this might work in business, it leaves little room for grace, sacrifice, or emotional depth in a relationship.

By contrast, an intentional relationship is built on presence, not performance. It prioritizes connection over conditions and love over leverage. You give not because it benefits you, but because you care. In an intentional model, both people are committed to each other’s growth, not just what they gain.
